title: Closure of Attributes
description: Compute attribute closures step by step, prove superkeys and minimal candidate keys, and test dependency implications without confusing sample data with invariants.

questions.question_text: What does computing {CourseID}+ over the running example's FD set yield?
options: All eight attributes of the relation
{CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice} — five attributes, missing the student-side and EnrollmentDate
Just {CourseID, CourseName}
{CourseID, StudentID, StudentName}
questions.explanation: CourseID reaches CourseName and InstructorID directly, then InstructorName and InstructorOffice transitively via InstructorID — but nothing determines StudentID, StudentName, or EnrollmentDate from CourseID alone.

questions.question_text: Why does {StudentID, CourseID}+ equal the entire set of eight attributes?
options: Because StudentID and CourseID are alphabetically first

Because starting from both together, every FD in the set can eventually be applied: StudentName and CourseName directly, InstructorID/Name/Office via the transitive chain, and EnrollmentDate via the composite-key FD
Because closures always equal all attributes
Because CourseID alone already reaches everything
questions.explanation: Every attribute is reachable: F1, F2, F3 apply immediately, F4/F5 apply once InstructorID is added, and F6 applies since both StudentID and CourseID are present from the start.

questions.question_text: In computing {StudentID, InstructorID}+, why does the closure NOT include CourseID?
options: Because CourseID is not part of any functional dependency

Because no FD in the set has a left-hand side reachable from {StudentID, InstructorID} that produces CourseID — InstructorID determines InstructorName/Office, not CourseID, since one instructor can teach multiple courses
Because StudentID and InstructorID are incompatible data types
Because CourseID must always be listed first in a closure
questions.explanation: The FD set only has CourseID -> InstructorID, never the reverse; nothing derives CourseID from InstructorID, so the closure of {StudentID, InstructorID} stops short of including it.

questions.question_text: What is the correct general algorithm for computing X+?
options: List every attribute in the relation regardless of FDs
Start with result = X; repeatedly scan all FDs and add an FD's right-hand side whenever its left-hand side is already a subset of result, until a pass adds nothing new
Apply only the first matching FD once and stop
Compute it by counting the number of candidate keys
questions.explanation: Closure computation is an iterative fixed-point process: keep re-scanning the whole FD set, adding newly-determined attributes, until no more can be added.

questions.question_text: Why is it a mistake to stop the closure computation for {CourseID}+ right after applying F2 and F3 (before checking F4 and F5)?
options: It is not a mistake — F4 and F5 never apply to CourseID's closure
F4 and F5 only become applicable AFTER InstructorID (added by F3) is already in the result, so stopping early would incorrectly omit InstructorName and InstructorOffice
Because F4 and F5 must always be applied before F2 and F3
Because closure computations must process FDs in numerical order only
questions.explanation: Closure requires repeated passes: F4 (InstructorID -> InstructorName) can't fire until InstructorID has been added to the result by F3, so an early stop would miss transitively reachable attributes.

questions.question_text: If X+ turns out to equal the full set of attributes of the relation, what can be concluded about X?
options: X is definitely a minimal candidate key
X is a superkey (it functionally determines every attribute), though it may or may not be minimal
X must be a foreign key
X cannot contain more than two attributes
questions.explanation: X+ = all attributes proves X is a superkey. Whether X is a candidate key additionally requires checking that no proper subset of X also has this property (21.10).

questions.question_text: Does the order in which applicable functional dependencies are applied during closure computation change the final result of X+?
options: Yes, applying FDs in a different order can yield a different final closure
No — as long as every applicable FD is eventually applied across repeated passes, the final closure is the same regardless of order
Yes, but only for composite determinants
No, because only one FD can ever apply to a given attribute set
questions.explanation: Closure is a deterministic fixed point; the order of applying applicable FDs doesn't matter, only that the process continues until no pass adds anything new.

questions.question_text: What is {StudentID}+ alone (ignoring CourseID) over the running example's FD set?
options: All eight attributes
{StudentID, StudentName} only, since no other FD has StudentID alone (without CourseID) on its left-hand side
{StudentID, CourseID, StudentName}
The empty set
questions.explanation: Only F1 (StudentID -> StudentName) has StudentID as a subset of its left-hand side without needing CourseID; F6 requires the composite {StudentID, CourseID}, which isn't available here.

questions.question_text: Can a closure algorithm apply AB→C when only A is available?
options: No, all determinant attributes are required
Yes, one is enough
Only for numeric columns
Always after sorting
questions.explanation: A composite determinant requires its complete left-hand side.

questions.question_text: What makes the closure algorithm terminate over a finite relation?
options: It deletes a row each time
Only finitely many attributes can be added
It guesses a fixed number of keys
It stops after the first dependency
questions.explanation: The set grows monotonically within a finite attribute universe.

questions.question_text: Does a superkey proof alone establish candidate-key minimality?
options: Yes, by definition
No
Only if a name column exists
Only if SQL returns no rows
questions.explanation: A superkey can contain removable attributes.

questions.question_text: What must a key contain if an attribute appears on no dependency right-hand side?
options: Only the first alphabetical attribute
No attributes
That attribute
Only a generated number
questions.explanation: Such an attribute cannot be derived unless supplied initially.

questions.question_text: How is X→Y implication tested?
options: Check whether X has fewer letters
Reverse every dependency
Count current table rows
Check whether Y is contained in X+
questions.explanation: Closure contains exactly the attributes determined under F.

questions.question_text: When testing whether one rule is redundant, which F should be used?
options: The remaining rules without that rule
Only the rule itself
An unrelated database schema
Every possible dependency
questions.explanation: A rule must not be allowed to prove its own redundancy.

questions.question_text: Can current sample uniqueness establish a dependency for every future legal state?
options: Yes, after one SELECT
No
Only if the sample is sorted
Only with short identifiers
questions.explanation: An instance observation is narrower than a domain invariant.

questions.question_text: Does A→B imply B→A automatically?
options: Yes, always
Only for text
No
Only after COMMIT
questions.explanation: Functional dependency is directional.

questions.question_text: For A→B, B→C, C→D, what is A+?
options: A only
B, C only
D only
A, B, C, D
questions.explanation: Repeated application reaches the full chain.

questions.question_text: After removing B→C from that chain, what is A+?
options: A, B
A, B, C, D
C, D
The empty set
questions.explanation: No remaining rule connects the available A, B set to C.

questions.question_text: What does COUNT(DISTINCT InstructorID) omit in the diagnostic?
options: Every repeated course row
NULL instructor values
Every nonnull identifier
All numeric values
questions.explanation: COUNT DISTINCT ignores NULL, so missingness needs separate treatment.

questions.question_text: What does inclusion-minimal candidate key mean?
options: It has the smallest identifier numbers
It uses every relation attribute
No proper subset remains a superkey
It has the shortest display label
questions.explanation: Minimality concerns removability rather than spelling or one global size.

notes:
## Find everything an attribute set determines

The closure of an attribute set X under functional dependencies F, written X+, is the set of attributes that X logically determines using those dependencies. It answers a precise question: starting with these known attributes, which other attributes must have a unique determined value in every legal relation satisfying F? The calculation uses declared dependencies, not the accidental distinctness of rows in one sample database.

Closure supports several design tasks. If X+ contains every attribute in a relation, X is a superkey. If Y is contained in X+, then F implies the dependency X determines Y. If removing an attribute from a superkey prevents full coverage, that removal does not preserve the superkey property. These uses connect one small fixed-point algorithm with key derivation, dependency simplification and normalization decisions.

## Write the relation and dependencies before calculating

Use an enrollment relation with eight attributes: StudentID, StudentName, CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice and EnrollmentDate. For this exercise, a student identifier determines the student's name, a course identifier determines the course name and assigned instructor, an instructor identifier determines the instructor name and office, and the student-course pair determines the enrollment date. These are assumptions about this designed domain, not universal facts about every school.

| Name | Dependency |
|---|---|
| F1 | StudentID → StudentName |
| F2 | CourseID → CourseName |
| F3 | CourseID → InstructorID |
| F4 | InstructorID → InstructorName |
| F5 | InstructorID → InstructorOffice |
| F6 | StudentID, CourseID → EnrollmentDate |

Changing the domain changes the calculation. If instructors can have several offices, the assumed instructor-to-office dependency is no longer justified without a more precise office rule. If a student can enroll in the same course several times, the proposed enrollment-date dependency may need a term or attempt identifier. A closure proof is valid relative to its stated dependency set; it cannot repair incorrect requirements.

## Run the repeated-addition algorithm

Initialize the result with X itself. Repeatedly inspect every dependency. When all attributes on a dependency's left side are already in the result, add its right-side attributes. Continue until a complete pass adds nothing. The left side must be contained as a whole; possessing one component of a composite determinant is insufficient. Additions are monotone, so the result grows but never loses attributes during this computation.

```text
result := X
repeat
    changed := false
    for each L → R in F:
        if L is a subset of result:
            add missing attributes of R to result
            if anything was added: changed := true
until changed is false
return result
```

With finitely many relation attributes, the process terminates after finitely many additions. The final set is a fixed point: every dependency whose determinant is available has already contributed its consequence. Different scanning orders can take different numbers of passes, but exhaustive repeated application reaches the same closure. Stopping after one convenient pass can miss a dependency enabled by an attribute added later in that pass.

## Trace a course identifier through the chain

Start with CourseID. F2 adds CourseName, and F3 adds InstructorID. The new instructor identifier enables F4 and F5, adding InstructorName and InstructorOffice. The final closure contains five attributes: the course identifier, course name, instructor identifier, instructor name and instructor office. It excludes StudentID, StudentName and EnrollmentDate because the given dependencies supply no route to the missing student identifier.

CourseID is therefore not a superkey for this eight-attribute relation. It does determine all the instructor attributes under these assumptions, even though those attributes are not listed directly on the right side of a course dependency. This illustrates transitivity operationally: the algorithm follows a chain without requiring every implied dependency to have been written explicitly in F.

Start instead with StudentID and InstructorID. F1 supplies StudentName, while F4 and F5 supply the instructor name and office. No dependency produces CourseID from that starting set. Knowing an instructor does not identify one course when that instructor may teach several. F6 cannot fire because its composite left side still lacks CourseID, so EnrollmentDate remains unavailable as well.

## Prove a candidate key rather than only a superkey

Starting from StudentID and CourseID reaches all eight attributes. The student identifier supplies StudentName, the course identifier supplies the course and instructor chain, and the complete pair supplies EnrollmentDate. This proves the pair is a superkey. It does not yet prove minimality: a superkey may contain attributes that are unnecessary for identifying all relation attributes.

Remove StudentID and the remaining CourseID closure has only five attributes. Remove CourseID and StudentID determines only itself and StudentName. Neither proper one-attribute subset is a superkey, so the pair is a candidate key. Minimal means inclusion-minimal, not necessarily the smallest cardinality among all possible keys. Different candidate keys in another relation can have different sizes while each lacks a removable attribute.

An attribute absent from every right-hand side cannot be generated by this algorithm unless it appears in the starting set. It must therefore belong to every superkey under the stated F. In this example both StudentID and CourseID have that property. Treat this as a useful necessity test, not a complete key-discovery algorithm: other relations can require choices among alternative determinants after all mandatory attributes are included.

## Use closure to test implications and simplifications

To test whether F implies X determines Y, compute X+ and check whether it contains Y. A composite right side requires every requested attribute to be present. If a proposed dependency is being tested for redundancy, compute the closure using the remaining dependency set after excluding that proposed rule. Leaving the rule in place would allow it to prove itself and would not establish redundancy.

Similarly, testing whether an attribute is extraneous in a determinant requires a carefully chosen closure test under the current dependencies. Distinguish that question from deleting an entire dependency. Simplification steps can change which later steps are valid, so recalculate using the actual current set. A minimal cover need not be unique, but a claimed replacement must preserve the original implications in both directions.

## Keep SQL observations separate from dependency proofs

A SQL GROUP BY check can find a current counterexample to a proposed dependency. If one CourseID appears with two different InstructorID values, the sample contradicts that dependency, subject to the chosen NULL and comparison semantics. Failure to find such a pair does not prove the dependency holds for every future legal state. Domain requirements and trusted enforcement establish the rule; current data can challenge it.

```sql
SELECT CourseID
FROM enrollment_sample
GROUP BY CourseID
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT InstructorID) > 1;
```

This diagnostic ignores NULL instructor values in COUNT DISTINCT, so its exact purpose must account for missingness. It is not an executable implementation of the symbolic closure algorithm, and it does not prove key minimality merely by returning no rows. Keep relational-theory dependencies distinct from SQL nullable uniqueness and from authorization rules governing who may inspect the sample.

## Consider empty determinants and irrelevant additions

The empty starting set is a legitimate mathematical input. If F contains an empty determinant determining a constant attribute, that attribute can be added even before any ordinary identifier is known. In the enrollment example no such rule exists, so the empty closure remains empty. State this assumption rather than claiming that every closure must always start with at least one attribute.

Adding an already determined attribute to X does not expand its closure beyond X+. Adding an unrelated attribute can expand the starting set without enabling any further rule. These observations help explain why a superkey containing many columns may still have only a much smaller candidate key hidden inside it.

## Solve two closure exercises

First exercise: compute StudentID+ and explain why adding InstructorName to the starting set still does not produce CourseID. The solution begins with StudentID and StudentName; adding a name supplies that attribute but no reverse dependency to InstructorID or CourseID. Dependency arrows cannot be reversed just because a display name happens to be unique in a small fixture.

Second exercise: let R contain A, B, C and D with A→B, B→C and C→D. Compute A+, then remove B→C and repeat. The first result contains all four attributes; the second contains only A and B. This comparison demonstrates why redundancy tests must exclude the candidate rule. Continue with [candidate-key derivation](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/candidate-key-derivation), [minimal covers](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/minimal-cover) and [BCNF](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/bcnf) to reuse the same disciplined reasoning.
